other_side: Zitron argues the AI build-out depends on debt that is getting more expensive: ten-year US Treasury yields above 5.3 per cent raise the floor for every data-centre borrower. He says the labs and builders will need at least $50 billion in new debt every year, probably at junk credit ratings, and he cites Oracle data-centre debt trading at 84 cents on the dollar. His point is that nobody can say who will pay for all this, and that the best-case assumption the market is making is dangerous.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is the cost and availability of capital against real AI revenue. They accept the facts: the build-out is huge, it is increasingly financed by private credit and lower-rated debt, and some lenders are asking for little detail. The empirical question is whether AI revenue grows into the debt service, and the observables that settle it are the pricing and take-up of Oracle's and SpaceX's financings, Treasury yields, and any downgrade. The worldview residue is whether revenue growth of the labs extrapolates. For Whittemore to be vindicated, lenders keep lending at tolerable rates and revenue arrives. For Zitron, funding tightens or a borrower is downgraded before revenue catches up. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore is bullish and anti-doom, Zitron is bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is where they agree despite opposite priors, that the financing is increasingly aggressive. Watch the outcome of the SpaceX chip loan.
